accepted.name: verified_satisfaction
accepted.description: Signed satisfaction (stars above or below the neutral 3) counted only when the review came from a verified purchase; unverified reviews contribute exactly 0 rather than an unearned opinion.
accepted.units: stars relative to neutral (3), purchase-verified only
accepted.why_it_matters: rating and verified are a measure and a provenance flag, not two measures. Averaging raw rating over a product's recent reviews mixes real buyers with the 30% unverified tail (promotional and non-purchase opinion). This is the quantity a person means by 'how happy are actual buyers right now', and credible dissatisfaction is what precedes a product's review stream drying up.

accepted.name: verified_complaint
accepted.description: Flag: a 1- or 2-star rating from a verified purchaser — a complaint backed by an actual purchase.
accepted.why_it_matters: ratings here are 50% five-star, so the informative event is the rare low rating; and a low rating with no purchase behind it is as likely to be a mistaken buyer or a competitor as a real defect. Summed over a product's recent window this is a defect/dissatisfaction count, the direct mechanism by which an item loses future demand and churns.

accepted.name: unverified_top_rating
accepted.description: Flag: a maximal 5-star rating from a reviewer with no verified purchase — the signature of incentivized, solicited or review-swap praise.
accepted.why_it_matters: the single most common row in this table is '5 stars, verified', so the diagnostic cell of the rating x verified cross is the opposite corner: top marks without a purchase. A product whose recent attention is mostly of this kind is being pushed rather than bought, and that attention stops when the push stops — a churn signal that raw mean rating actively hides, because it looks identical to genuine excellence.

accepted.name: verified_rating_mass
accepted.description: Star mass contributed only by purchase-verified reviews: the rating if the purchase was verified, 0 otherwise.
accepted.why_it_matters: a product-level aggregate of this over a window, read against the count of verified rows, is the verified-only average rating — the quality number a shopper would actually trust. It is a product of two columns, so no pairwise difference or ratio of numeric columns reaches it, and unlike verified_satisfaction it preserves the absolute star level rather than only the sign around neutral.

accepted.name: verified_polarization
accepted.description: How far a verified purchaser's rating sits from neutral, regardless of direction: intensity of credible opinion.
accepted.why_it_matters: intensity and valence are different things and churn responds to both. A stream of credible 3-star 'it was fine' reviews is a product drifting into indifference; strong feeling in either direction means the item still provokes buyers. Pairing this with verified_satisfaction separates 'nobody cares' from 'people care and are unhappy', which a mean rating cannot distinguish.

accepted.name: rating_extremity
accepted.description: Distance of the star rating from the neutral midpoint: 0 for a 3-star review, 2 for a 1- or 5-star review.
accepted.why_it_matters: the 1-5 scale is not a measurement axis that should be read linearly; its middle is 'no strong opinion' and both ends are engagement. This folds the scale at its own midpoint, which is not a rescaling of rating (it is non-monotone: 1 and 5 map together), and gives a product-level 'does this item still provoke a reaction' feature that is orthogonal to its average score.

accepted.name: price_cents
accepted.description: The sub-dollar part of the list price — the cents ending alone (0.99, 0.95, 0.00, ...).
accepted.why_it_matters: only 8,679 distinct prices cover 506k products because real retail prices snap to psychological endings. The cents ending is therefore not noise but a marker of who set the price: a .99/.95 ending is an actively merchandised consumer item, an arbitrary ending is typically a marketplace or third-party listing. It carries none of price's magnitude, so it is not a rescaling, and it survives the enormous right tail (max $5,204) that distorts every ratio involving price.

accepted.name: is_round_dollar_priced
accepted.description: Flag: a priced item whose list price is a whole number of dollars ($10.00, $25.00), excluding the 0.0 missing-price sentinel.
accepted.why_it_matters: round-dollar pricing is the fingerprint of non-retail pricing — institutional, print-on-demand, bundled or hand-entered listings — as opposed to the charm pricing that dominates a merchandised catalogue. Those items collect reviews slowly and stop collecting them early, so this is a cold-start/churn prior available from a product's own static row with no history at all. The `price > 0` guard is load-bearing: 0.0 is a sentinel and would otherwise be counted as the roundest price of all.

accepted.name: price_is_missing
accepted.description: Flag: the list price is the 0.0 sentinel, i.e. no price was recorded for this product — not a free item.
accepted.why_it_matters: price has a 0% null rate but a hard 0.0 floor, so its missingness is encoded in-band and every mean, ratio or difference the brute-force generator builds from price silently treats 'unknown' as 'free'. Made explicit, the flag is also informative in its own right: an unpriced catalogue row is usually delisted, out of print or never properly ingested, and such items are exactly the ones whose review stream ends.
